question: Poland has been criticised many times for persecuting people for their political opinions and holding them in detention without trial. The case of Mateusz Piskorski, however, stands apart. Piskorski, a political scientist and journalist, is a former member of the Polish Sejm and founder of the Zmiana party.

He was arrested in May 2016 on charges of spying for Russia and China, and on account of his public activities – demonstrations, protests and political activism. He spent nearly three years behind bars, including two years in pretrial detention. Piskorski denies the charges and the case is still ongoing. He was released on bail, but remains under police supervision and cannot leave Poland.

The ban on his political activities has now been lifted by a court. In its Opinion A/HRC/WGAD/2018/18 of 20 April 2018, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention – an independent, five-member expert panel of the UN Human Rights Council – described Piskorski’s detention as arbitrary on the grounds of violation of freedom of expression, freedom of association and the right to a fair trial.
It called on Poland immediately to release him, award compensation and launch an independent investigation into the case. 1.

The Commission criticises various countries for persecuting political opponents, but it applies a different standard when its own Member States are responsible. Is it planning to comment on the Piskorski case?
Would it not be better to tone down criticism of political conditions in countries like China, Belarus and Cuba, and instead look first at conditions in its own ranks?
